scenes.title: Hobson
lines: A text adventure with two brains.
Amazon Nova writes the story. Strands Decider 2B decides what is true in it.
Nothing about the story is written in advance: you type where it begins, and what you do.
An LLM game master believes whatever the player asserts. Hobson gives the believing to a model that cannot write.
scenes.vo: Here is the problem, in one turn. The player claims a brass key, an uncle, and a locked cabinet. Nothing in this story has ever mentioned any of them. Hand that turn to a language model, and this is what it actually wrote: the brass key, gripped tightly in your hand. The key now exists. The player edited the world by saying so. Hobson gives the deciding to Strands Decider 2B, a model that cannot write a sentence. No key. And nothing from this turn is recorded.
Four things: a world nobody wrote, an honest turn, a bluff, and the measurements.

scenes.title: Every turn, Decider answers
lines: What did you try?              free text -> one of nine fixed categories
Is that true in the story?     each claim, checked against the ledger
Do you actually have that?     each item named, checked against the ledger
What happens?                  one of four outcomes Nova just proposed
Does the writing keep to the facts?
Nova's paragraph, checked before it counts
Under 60%, Decider says "not sure" and Nova takes that call.
scenes.vo: So what is the small model actually for? Closed questions with a confidence on each. Five a turn: what did you try, is each claim true so far, do you hold what you named, which outcome follows, and does Nova's paragraph keep to the facts. Under sixty percent sure, Decider says so and hands that call to Nova.
Nothing is written in advance. I type a premise, and Nova builds the place and the opening facts. Type a payments outage or a generation ship instead, and it does the same. We ran both.

scenes.action: I set the lamp down and finally open the letter
scenes.vo: An honest turn. I open the letter. Nova extracts what it leans on: a lamp, a letter. Both are in the record, so both pass, and what happens is written down.

scenes.action: I use the brass key my uncle gave me to open the locked cabinet by the lamp
scenes.vo: Now the bluff. A brass key my uncle gave me, a locked cabinet. None of it exists anywhere in this story.

Refused. Every claim checked against the record and found missing, around eighty percent sure. And the record underneath does not move, so the next turn cannot build on it. With Nova Lite refereeing instead, the key was believed in two runs out of three.

Same script, two referees, three runs each. Decider refused eleven of twenty-two player claims; Nova Lite, eight of twenty-four. The brass-key bluff: Decider refused it three times out of three, Nova Lite believed the key in two. Same ruling time, Decider's share under two seconds, at no API cost. On open picks Decider is often not sure, and says so. On yes or no against a record, it is the one you want.
lines: Decider cannot be talked into anything, and says "not sure" when it is.
Nova writes, proposes, and takes the open calls. results/md/referee_compare.md
scenes.title: Two referees, three runs each
Hobson
lines: Strands Decider 2B on the Mac · Amazon Nova Lite and Pro on Amazon Bedrock
Decision pattern: #guardrails. The ledger guard is one typed question and ten lines of wiring, reusable anywhere a generator is allowed to act on what a user asserts.
scenes.vo: Which is the useful part, and it is not about games. Any agent acting on what a user tells it has this problem: refunds, claims, access, support. So the guard ships on its own, as a Strands intervention handler, with a refund desk that refuses an order never delivered and asks a human when unsure. The pattern is guardrails.

premise: a lighthouse on the Kerala coast during a storm, 1962; I am the keeper's niece, sent up with a lamp and a letter I have not read
